Arleigh Kraus Warren LD 1831
May 5, 2025 LD 1831
Testimony in Support of LD 1831 An Act Requiring Disclosure and Oversight of Radiation and Ozonation Treatments in Adult Use Cannabis Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs. My name is Arleigh Kraus, and I am writing to express my support for this bill, which ensures transparency and consumer safety in Maine's adult use cannabis market by requiring disclosure of radiation and ozonation treatments, and the inspection and registration of equipment used for such processes. Requiring clear labeling of cannabis products that have been subject to radiation treatment or ozonation empowers consumers to make informed decisions. Just as we expect transparency in food labeling, patients and adult-use consumers deserve to know if their cannabis has undergone these processes, which may affect product quality, cannabinoid profile, or perceived safety. This disclosure is not only a matter of consumer rights--it fosters trust in the regulated cannabis market. Mandating inspection and registration of radiation and ozonation equipment by the Office of Cannabis Policy introduces a necessary layer of safety and accountability. These technologies, while potentially effective for microbial control, must be used responsibly and safely. Proper oversight ensures that their use aligns with best practices and public health standards, while preventing misuse or unregulated experimentation. This bill does not ban the use of these methods--it simply requires transparency and proper regulatory oversight. It supports both consumer choice and industry responsibility, and reflects the thoughtful, science-informed policy Maine is known for. I urge the Committee to vote "Ought to Pass" and help advance Maine's commitment to safety, integrity, and informed choice in the cannabis industry. Thank you for the opportunity to testify. Respectfully, Arleigh Kraus

Testimony of Rep. David Boyer introducing LD 1831, An Act to Support Small Adult Use Cannabis Businesses by Establishing a Micro Cannabis Facility License Before the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs
May 8, 2025
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and esteemed colleagues of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee, my name is David Boyer, and I am proud to introduce LD 1831, An Act to Support Small Adult Use Cannabis Businesses by Establishing a Micro Cannabis Facility License. This bill would create a micro license which would allow small cultivators to be vertically integrated. This means they would be able to cultivate, manufacture, and retail cannabis, if they are in a municipality that allows for it and they are zoned accordingly. This is similar to how caregivers are vertically integrated in the medical program. This would save small operators thousands of dollars on license fees every year. Additionally, it would exempt small operators from the adult-use excise tax. Right now, the excise tax is one of the biggest reasons medical operators have chosen not to transition into the adult-use program. I would argue that state revenue would increase if this option were available, as it would encourage more participation in the adult-use cannabis industry. I appreciate the committee's time and consideration on this matter. Thank you.

Re: LD 1831, An Act to Support Small Adult Use Cannabis Businesses by Establishing a Micro Cannabis Facility License

Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs:

The Office of Cannabis Policy (OCP) respectfully submits the following comments neither for nor against LD 1831 to provide the committee with information to consider regarding the establishment of micro cannabis facilities as a new adult use cannabis establishment license type.

The micro cannabis facilities proposed in this bill would be permitted to participate in the cultivation (up to 1,000 square feet), manufacture, and sale of adult use cannabis and cannabis products to consumers all through one license type. This approach is comparable to the registered caregiver and registered dispensary models in Maine's medical cannabis program, where those registrants can conduct a number of authorized activities under one registration type. This does, however, vary from the current licensing structure in the adult use program where cultivation facilities, products manufacturing facilities, and cannabis stores are each licensed separately and specific to the authorized activity being conducted at that facility.

While the Office is generally supportive of the creation of a new micro cannabis facility license, it is imperative that those licensees be held to the same standards for inventory tracking, mandatory testing, local authorization, and taxation as all other adult use cannabis licensees across the state. At present, this bill does specify that micro cannabis facilities shall track all adult use cannabis and cannabis products from seed to sale. It also makes clear that micro cannabis facilities would be "subject to the same requirements and restrictions" applicable to existing cultivation facilities, products manufacturing facilities, and cannabis stores. It is the Office's expectation that those provisions would extend the mandatory testing standards and local authorization requirements applicable to other adult use cannabis establishments to micro cannabis facilities.

This bill does maintain parity when it comes to the sales tax, requiring micro cannabis facilities that sell adult use cannabis and cannabis products to consumers to collect and pay to the State Tax Assessor the applicable sales tax, as is required of adult use cannabis stores. However, adult use cannabis cultivated and sold by micro cannabis facilities would not be subject to the excise tax on adult use cannabis applicable to all other adult use cultivation facilities. This would offer a significant advantage to micro cannabis facility cultivators over other cultivators, particularly those Tier 1 and Tier 2 cultivators operating at a similar scale yet still being subject to excise tax - all of which raises constitutional concerns around equal application of the laws governing the taxation of cannabis. That being said, the Office continues to support a reduction of the excise tax for all adult use cannabis cultivation facilities across the board.

10054205:
Kimber Duncan Lisbon Falls LD 1831
Good Morning Senator, Hickman, Representative Supica, and distinguished members of the joint committee on Veteran and Legal Affairs. My name is Kimber Duncan and I live in Lisbon Falls. I am the general manager of a small cultivator that entered into adult-use in 2020 and is no longer in adult-use as of October 2024.
I strongly SUPPORT this bill. I think the barrier to entry in adult-use is much higher than med. It makes sense that this license should not pay the excise taxes the other licenses pay. I think those taxes are too much and it ruined the ability for the company I work for to stay in adult use. The biggest contributing factor to us leaving the adult-use market was the excise taxes.
A couple items to note about these excise taxes and the burden the pose on small licenses -
Cannabis excise tax needs to be paid on the 15th for the previous month's sales. So if I sell product on the 31st and it is billed as Net 30, I have not received that money yet but I need to pay the excise taxes on the order. If I don't I will incur penalties and interest will accrue on this tax bill making the bill larger.
If a business is not caught up with excise taxes and/or they are not on a payment plan with MRS, it affects their ability to renew their adult-use license.
MRS is not willing to work with companies beyond putting them on a no-wiggle-room payment plan. The requirements of a payment plan with MRS are that it not be more than 12 months in duration, and the company must pay all future excise tax bills on time in order to stay on the plan. e.g. if my plan covers Jan-March, I need to pay April and May on time while also paying off Jan-March to stay in good standing. When we couldn't pay one of these upcoming bills in full but needed to stay on the plan, we proactively called MRS for help. We literally didn't have the money in the account to do both taxes and payroll as they both came out on the same day and a check we were waiting for hadn't come in on time, so we asked what to do and how they could help us stay in good standing - if we could slide the due date a few days or something. They suggested not paying payroll this round in order to pay our tax bill and had nothing more to offer for suggestions or sympathy.
I request that you to vote in SUPPORT of this bill LD-1831- An Act to Support Small Adult Use Cannabis Businesses by Establishing a Micro Cannabis Facility License.
Thank you for your time reading this testimony.
Best regards,
Kimber Duncan
10055791:
TESTIMONY OF MICHAEL J. ALLEN, ASSOCIATE COMMISSIONER FOR TAX POLICY
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE AND FINANCIAL SERVICES
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs Hearing Date: May 8, 2025
LD 1831 - "An Act to Support Small Adult Use Cannabis Businesses by Establishing a Micro Cannabis Facility License"
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and members of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee - good morning, my name is Michael Allen, Associate Commissioner for Tax Policy in the Department of Administrative and Financial Services. I am testifying at the request of the Administration Neither For Nor Against LD 1831, "An Act to Support Small Adult Use Cannabis Businesses by Establishing a Micro Cannabis Facility License."
This testimony is limited to the bill's effect on taxation. This bill would amend the Cannabis Legalization Act to establish a micro cannabis facility license, which would permit the cultivation of up to 1,000 square feet of plant canopy, and the licensee would be permitted to sell and distribute cultivated and manufactured adult use cannabis to other licensed establishments, as well as sell adult use cannabis, adult use cannabis products, immature cannabis plants, and seedlings to consumers under this single license. Adult use cannabis cultivated and sold under this license would not be subject to the otherwise applicable cannabis excise tax thereby incentivizing current adult use cannabis licensed establishments to restructure their businesses to operate under the new license.
In addition to the testimony provided by the Office of Cannabis Policy, the Department would like to raise the following technical issues for consideration by the Committee.
1

The bill is unclear on whether a micro cannabis facility licensee may only manufacture and sell self-cultivated products or whether it may also receive cannabis from another licensee. In addition, it is unclear whether the bill exempts only a micro cannabis facility's sales of self-cultivated cannabis from the cannabis excise tax or whether it exempts all cannabis sold by a micro cannabis facility (that sells any amount of self-cultivated cannabis).
From a drafting standpoint, it would be preferable if the bill clearly described and enacted any exemption from the cannabis excise tax for micro cannabis facilities under Title 36, chapter 723 (Cannabis Excise Tax).
The Administration looks forward to working with the Committee on the bill.

10053487:
Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association In Opposition To
LD 1831 - An Act to Support Small Adult Use Cannabis Businesses by Establishing a Micro Cannabis Facility License May 8, 2025
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and members of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee, my name is Rebecca Lambert, and I am providing testimony in opposition to LD 1831 on behalf of the Maine Municipal Association's (MMA) elected 70-member Legislative Policy Committee (LPC). For reference, MMA is a nonpartisan, nonprofit member service organization and aims to help provide policy solutions that work for all residents in Maine and the LPC guides MMA's advocacy efforts and establishes positions on bills of municipal interest.
Municipal officials respectfully oppose the creation of a new adult use micro cannabis facility license as proposed in this bill. While local leaders recognize the intent to create pathways for small-scale operators to enter the market, the proposed license type is redundant and unnecessary.
Under Maine's existing adult use cannabis law, the Tier 1 cultivation license already allows for very small-scale commercial cultivation, with canopy limits that are smaller than what is being proposed under the new micro facility license. This existing license type was designed specifically to accommodate entrylevel cultivators and provide an on-ramp into the legal market. Adding a new and overlapping license category not only creates confusion for applicants and regulators but undermines the consistency and clarity that both the state and municipalities have worked hard to build.
If the intent of LD 1831 is to address issues with the accessibility of Tier 1 licenses, whether due to fees, application process, or zoning barriers, those challenges should be addressed within the existing framework and not through the introduction of new, duplicative license types.
For opt in municipalities tasked with reviewing and approving cannabis businesses, each new license type introduces administrative burdens, enforcement challenges, and potential zoning changes. Local ordinances, land use regulations, and permitting procedures must be reviewed and possibly revised to account for new license classes. This is not a small undertaking, particularly for small towns with limited staff and legal resources.
For these reasons, local leaders are opposed to the creation of a new adult use micro cannabis facility license. They appreciate the intent to expand access and support smaller operators, but ultimately believe this bill addresses the wrong problem with the wrong tool.
Thank you for your time and considering the municipal perspective.
